1:
The evil named at the opening is having without using. Matthew Henry reads the chapter as the counterpart of what went before, where the comfortable use of God’s gifts was commended: here is the man who gathers to lay up against contingencies to come and will not lay out on the urgent occasion present. He makes two observations on the phrase under the sun. There is a world above it where no evil is, and God causes his sun to shine on the evil as well as the good, which he counts an aggravation of this one; and the preacher, as a king inspecting the manners of his subjects, saw the practice as a prejudice to the public, damaged by penuriousness as much as by prodigality—for as it is with the blood in the natural body, so with the wealth of the body politic, which if it stagnates instead of circulating will be of ill consequence. He adds that no providence of itself will cure the corrupt affection for the world, since when riches increase we are most apt to set our hearts on them. Charles Ellicott corrects the rendering of the first line, preferring heavy upon to common among, and states the theme of the section: that riches may remain with a man to the end of his life and still fail to bring him any real happiness. John Gill notes that one old version makes this a second and different evil, and thinks it wrong, since the covetousness of the preceding chapter is still in view.

The gifts themselves are carefully sorted. Gill distinguishes the terms—gold and silver by the first, cattle and stock by the second, since in that age and country wealth lay largely in herds—and grants that all three are God’s gifts, though a curse may go along with them. Charles Ellicott notes that the same three words are used together of the king to whom the book is ascribed. Henry sets out the same point as a series: riches commonly gain a man honour, since though it be an image, if it be a golden image all nations will fall down before it; riches and honour are the gifts of providence, and not given like rain and sunshine alike to all, but to some and not to others; and they are given to many who are denied the grace to take the comfort of them, so that the gifts of common providence often do more hurt than good where the gifts of special grace are withheld.

Why the owner cannot eat is where the voices differ. Adam Clarke makes it a general truth about the human condition—possession and fruition are not necessarily joined together, and it belongs to God as much to give the power of enjoying as to give the thing enjoyed—and observes that a heathen poet saw as much, who wrote that the gods had given a man riches and the art of using them as two separate gifts. John Wesley makes the withholding judicial: the man cannot eat because God has given him up to a base and covetous mind. Keil and Delitzsch work on the wording rather than the cause. They refuse a translation that would give, and there is nothing wanting to him, on the ground that the pronoun cannot be made to carry it, and they take the clause to mean that he lacks for his own person nothing of all he desires. Of the stranger who comes into the estate at last they say only, but firmly, that he is certainly not the legal heir—which leaves the sting in the verse where the preacher put it, that the whole provision passes to someone with no claim on it at all.
3:
The detail that most exercises them is the missing burial. Keil and Delitzsch report a scholar who found the clause so awkward that he took it for a marginal note on a later verse wandered into the text at the wrong place; they answer that its very unexpectedness, its air of accident rather than inward necessity, suggests the author is fitting real facts into a single imagined portrait. Charles Ellicott reaches the same suspicion from the other end: that a man should be so busy pursuing riches as never to enjoy them is common enough, but that the same man should also be left without a sepulchre to keep his name need not follow, so one is tempted to think the Preacher has some actual occurrence in mind. Adam Clarke removes the puzzle by making the want of a grave deliberate—the man is so attached to his riches that he grudges himself a monument—and concludes he is contemptible and his life worthless. John Gill takes the hundred children as a round number, citing two kings of the histories who came near it, and notes such a family was reckoned great honour and happiness, which is what makes the comparison severe. John Wesley supplies the ground of it, that the untimely birth never enjoyed the comforts of life and equally never felt its calamities.

Who is described in the fourth verse is disputed. Gill sets out three possibilities without settling them: that the coming in with vanity and departing in darkness belongs to the untimely birth, which is nevertheless preferred to the covetous man; that it belongs to the covetous man himself; or that the two may be compared in these very terms, since the rich man also walks in a vain show and is vanity in his coming in, his life and his going out. Ellicott decides it in four words, that the subject is not he but it, the untimely birth. Keil and Delitzsch fill the picture in. It entered existence in nothingness, what it entered being a lifeless existence where independent life should have begun; it departs in darkness, carried away without noise or ceremony; and darkness covers its name, for it receives none and is forgotten as though it had never been. On their reading the deprivation is itself the advantage: never having seen the sun or known it, it is spared the sight of all the vanities and evils, the deceptions and sorrows, that are under the sun.

The thousand years doubled draw both textual and theological comment. Gill observes that no man ever lived even one such span, the oldest on record falling well short, and reports a people said to live half as long again as usual, which one authority puts at twice the common term; he notes too a Jewish reading making the phrase a thousand thousand, which he thinks wrong, and an Arabic version giving many thousand years. Ellicott adds that the conjunction opening the verse occurs only once elsewhere. Keil and Delitzsch concede the argument and then mark its limit. A life of that length without enjoyment is indeed worthless, they say, and would be so on any reckoning if the good meant were understood inwardly and spiritually; but though the fear of God presides over the enjoyment of life in this book, regulating and hallowing it, the author does not appear to know that a life deepened into fellowship with God is itself the most real and blessed thing, and so the highest good of all. Wesley draws the practical conclusion instead, that where no comfort has been enjoyed a long life is rather a curse than a blessing, and that the closing question levels the two, since all go to one place whether their lives be long or short.
7:
The first of these verses is read as a statement about appetite rather than food. Keil and Delitzsch refuse a reading that sets mouth and soul in contrast as the organs of merely sensual and of deeper spiritual joys, saying it brings out of the text what it wishes to find there: the two stand so little opposed that the stomach could have been named instead, since what is meant is the soul longing after the means of its own preservation. They add that in the rabbinic phrase a beautiful soul means an appetite not fastidious but contented. Matthew Henry gives it edge—meats are for the belly and the belly for meats, and there is nothing here for the head and heart—and adds two reasons why the appetite is never filled: natural desires always return, so a man feasted today is hungry tomorrow, and sinful desires are insatiable, wealth being to a worldling what drink is to a man in a dropsy. Henry also reports an alternative rendering of the whole verse, that though all a man’s labour fall out exactly to his own mind, his desire is still not satisfied. Adam Clarke draws the conclusion, that when a man learns to provide as distinctly for his soul as for his body he will begin to be happy.

The next verse defeats the scholars, and they say so plainly. Keil and Delitzsch report that the old translators contribute nothing to it and merely defend the traditional text, one following a Jewish reading that takes the living for the blessed future, contrary, they say, to the spirit of the book. The question would be easier, they allow, if a comparative particle could be introduced; but then the man who knows how to walk before the living would have to be someone acting a part in public life, and they ask what a strange designation for distinguished persons that is. As it stands, the participle is an attribute of the poor man himself. Charles Ellicott confesses the same difficulty in a sentence: the phrase means understanding how to conduct oneself, but why this should be limited to the poor is not obvious. Clarke and John Gill keep the plain sense, Clarke observing that a rich man can no more eat two meals at once than wear two changes of raiment, so the necessaries of life are the same for both, and both liable to the same diseases and death. Henry allows the equality and qualifies it: suppose the two equal in possessions, and neither can squeeze more than needful supplies from an estate, so that but for the pleasures peculiar to the mind they would be level as to this world.

On the last verse the dispute is again about a word. Keil and Delitzsch reject a rendering making the phrase an impulse or rush of the appetite, since the verb bears that sense only with subjects such as fire or contagion and in forms that do not apply here; they take it as a roving out to a distance, and observe that going is the contrast of rest, the soul never filled goes out to seek and never reaches it. Clarke quotes the Latin version as an adage—better to see what one desires than covet what one does not know—then stops at the literal words, which give the travelling of the soul, and asks what that is: whether it means only desire, or refers to the state of separate spirits. He does not answer, saying only that it shows the soul restless and unhappy, and that where Christ dwells by faith the soul is at rest. Gill guards the first half: the sight of the eyes here is not the bare beholding of riches but the enjoyment of present mercies, while the wandering desire enlarges itself as hell and covets everything under the sun. John Wesley states both halves briefly.
10:
The tenth verse is admitted to be hard. Charles Ellicott says so outright, saying that of this difficult verse he prefers one translation among several—the name given long ago to man indicates his weakness—and adds that the word for the stronger party occurs only in the Chaldee portions of the Bible and in later Hebrew. Keil and Delitzsch shift the verse from the sphere of events to that of decree: the tense really gives that whatever has appeared had its name named long ago, its What and its How determined and, so to speak, formulated in advance. They reject a repunctuation, made against the accents, giving, it is known that if one is a man he cannot contend, and call the construction it requires impossible. John Gill and Adam Clarke both find the first man there, Clarke reading it as question and answer—who is he who is? his name has been called already, and it is known that he is the man of earth—and drawing from it his dignity, his fall, his recovery. Gill reports that some refer the words to the second man, the Lord from heaven, one old version reading not that which has been but that which shall be. John Wesley makes the naming purposive: it was given that a man might always be sensible of his vain estate.

Whether the eleventh verse speaks of things or words is the next question. Keil and Delitzsch argue for words, since the contending of the previous verse is carried on in speech, and name commentators who take the other view; their reading turns the line into a comment on argument itself: wrestling against God’s decree being worthless, many words only increase the vanities already in the world. They go further and find in it a trace of the schools existing in the author’s time, recalling the controversy between the parties over human freedom and divine absoluteness. Matthew Henry treats the verse as the conclusion the book has been proving, and infers that a man is never the nearer to happiness for his abundance, since when he balances his accounts there is no overplus that will turn to any account. His second inference answers the verse that follows: we do not know what to wish for, since what we promise ourselves most satisfaction in often proves most vexatious—it is a mark of our corruption that we desire as good what is really hurtful, like children crying for knives to cut their fingers with.

On the closing question they agree, and Adam Clarke puts it most plainly. The things we deem good are often evil and those we think evil often good, so that in our ignorance we run the greatest hazard in choosing, and it is better to leave ourselves in God’s hands than keep ourselves in our own. Of the second half he is blunter: futurity is with God; while he lives a man wishes to know what is before him, and when he is about to die what will be after him, and God, because he is merciful, will reveal neither. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same place another way: a man ought to fear God and submit without dispute or murmuring, since to tell him what is good for him would mean settling what position he should take, what direction to give his activity, and what to decide in hard cases. Wesley draws the double ignorance: no man knows whether it is better to be high or low, rich or poor, and as he can have no contentment in these things while he lives, neither can he in leaving them, knowing neither who will possess them nor how they will be used. Gill turns it into counsel—since no man knows what is best for him, the wisest way is to be content with what he has—and Ellicott notes only the figure of the shadow.
